title: The 2008 recession 10 years on
meta_description: A decade after the beginning of the recession, how has the UK economy recovered?
lede: A decade after the beginning of the recession, how has the UK economy recovered?

body.text: 30 April 2018

body.h4: This is what a recession looks like…
body.text: This is what a recession looks like…

body.h4: This is what a recession looks like…
body.text: Since 1992, the size of the UK economy, measured by adding up the value of all the goods and services produced in the country, had been getting bigger every quarter. But in April to June 2008, it began to fall.

body.h4: This is what a recession looks like…
body.text: The economy kept getting smaller for five successive quarters. Two or more consecutive quarters of falling gross domestic product (GDP) is commonly called a recession.

body.h4: GDP took five years to recover
body.text: GDP took five years to recover

body.h4: GDP took five years to recover
body.text: Having shrunk by more than 6% between the first quarter of 2008 and the second quarter of 2009, the UK economy took five years to get back to the size it was before the recession. The latest data show that the UK economy is now 11% bigger than it was before the recession.

body.h4: Unemployment reached its highest rate since 1995
body.text: Unemployment reached its highest rate since 1995

body.h4: Unemployment reached its highest rate since 1995
body.text: As the economy got smaller, lots of people lost their jobs and employers stopped hiring. By the end of 2011, almost 2.7 million people were looking for work. The quarterly unemployment rate reached 8.4%, the highest rate since 1995.

body.h4: Unemployment reached its highest rate since 1995
body.text: Unemployment had returned to its pre-downturn rate at the end of 2015, and since then it has continued to fall – reaching a record low of 4.3% in the third quarter of 2017 before rising slightly at the end of the year.

body.h4: Earnings haven't kept up with prices
body.text: Earnings haven't kept up with prices

body.h4: Earnings haven't kept up with prices
body.text: Earnings have lagged behind prices for most of the decade since the start of the recession.

body.h4: Earnings haven't kept up with prices
body.text: In the public sector, a pay freeze (from 2011) and pay cap (from 2013) kept wage rises below inflation, while in the private sector wage growth was also slow.

body.h4: Earnings haven't kept up with prices
body.text: There was a two-year period beginning around July 2014 when wages rose in real terms – this was due largely to the fall in the price of oil causing prices to come down too.

body.h4: Earnings haven't kept up with prices
body.text: However, between November 2015 and October 2016, the pound fell in value by 20%, including a record 6.5% fall between June and July 2016 following the EU referendum. This meant it was more expensive to import goods and services, so prices rose and earnings are again failing to keep up with prices.

body.h4: The productivity puzzle
body.text: The productivity puzzle

body.h4: The productivity puzzle
body.text: One way to measure the strength of the economy is looking at how much money each worker adds to the economy – their labour productivity, measured in output per hour.

body.h4: The productivity puzzle
body.text: Productivity had been rising steadily before the recession, but it slumped in 2008 and has barely recovered since. Had the pre-2008 trend continued, productivity would have been 20% higher than it actually was at the end of 2017.

body.h4: The productivity puzzle
body.text: Lots of reasons have been suggested for this, including banks not being willing to lend to new businesses, low levels of business investment and companies being able to keep staff on instead of making them redundant, because wages have not been rising.

body.h4: The productivity puzzle
body.text: But the phenomenon of low productivity growth, common to many economies across Europe, is not fully understood and has been called the “productivity puzzle”.
